description:
We are a team of Electrical and Electronics Engineering students from Kumasi Technical University in Ghana, passionate about transforming complex data into impactful innovations. 

By integrating our skills in data sourcing, web development and research, our goal is to design a web application that sources out data from NASA's dataset combined with local Agricultural data to help Ghanaian farmers make informed decisions that can maximize crop yield and reduce losses.
summary: We built a website that collects data from NASA's dataset combined with data from the Ministry of Food and Agriculture, Ghana to advise farmers on the best crop rotation and agricultural practices due the current climate condition
details:
AgroSync: Agricultural Intelligence for Ghana is a web-based farm decision-support platform designed to translate satellite Earth observations and localized weather models into practical, everyday guidance for Ghanaian farmers. Through an interactive Farm Decision Dashboard, users can select their administrative region (such as the Eastern Region), input specific farm latitude and longitude coordinates, or capture their real-time position via device geolocation to retrieve environmental readings tailored to their exact locality. Rather than presenting raw meteorological numbers in isolation, AgroSync synthesizes multi-source environmental telemetry—including air temperature, relative humidity, derived National Weather Service heat index, 24-hour rainfall totals, NASA POWER evapotranspiration, surface soil moisture, and NASA/USGS SRTM terrain slope—into clear, actionable field advisories.

Beyond environmental monitoring, the platform works by connecting real-time field conditions directly to crop phenology and long-term soil management. In the Agricultural Recommendation module, a farmer selects a specific crop and its current growth stage—such as tomatoes in the maturing and harvest stage—and immediately receives context-aware instructions. For instance, when recent rainfall is detected alongside high humidity, the system advises farmers to clear blocked drains before adding water, inspect mature fruit for post-rain cracking, check valley bottoms and heavy-soil patches for root waterlogging, and maintain healthy plant residues on sloped terrain to prevent runoff. Complementing these immediate actions, the Crop Rotation Planner evaluates a farmer's current crop, planned successor crop (such as transitioning from cabbage to pepper), main resource priority (like conserving water), soil texture, water availability, and sowing dates to generate tailored rotation recommendations. AgroSync also incorporates Registration and Broadcast modules to support wider farmer onboarding and community-level advisory distribution.

The primary benefit of AgroSync is that it gives smallholder farmers access to precision agrometeorological intelligence without requiring expensive on-farm weather stations or specialized technical training. By distilling complex satellite and weather parameters into plain-language steps, the platform helps farmers optimize irrigation, minimize post-rain crop spoilage, protect topsoil on sloped plots, and make informed crop-sequencing decisions. The intended impact of the project is to strengthen climate resilience, improve water-use efficiency, and protect crop yields across Ghana’s farming communities while reinforcing grassroots agricultural support networks by encouraging farmers to validate seed availability and planting schedules with local Ministry of Food and Agriculture (MoFA) extension officers.

To develop and deploy AgroSync, we combined lightweight web technologies, AI-assisted research and engineering tools, and open Earth-observation APIs. The frontend interface was built using HTML5, CSS3, and JavaScript (index.html and style.css), styled with a high-contrast dark theme to ensure legibility under bright outdoor sunlight. On the data layer, the application integrates the NASA POWER API for modeled evapotranspiration, NASA/USGS SRTM elevation data for terrain slope screening, Open-Meteo models for air temperature, relative humidity, 24-hour precipitation, and surface soil moisture, as well as the browser Geolocation API for coordinate capture. During development, we used Gemini for background research—synthesizing agronomic best practices, NASA satellite dataset documentation, and agrometeorological equations—and wrote the codebase inside Visual Studio Code with Codex serving as an AI coding assistant to accelerate code generation, API integration, and debugging. Source-code management was handled with Git and GitHub, while Netlify (agrosyncgh.netlify.app) provided continuous cloud hosting and deployment, with testing conducted across standard laptops and mobile smartphones.

AgroSync’s creativity lies in how it bridges scientific honesty with grassroots usability. Most agricultural apps display raw numbers as absolute measurements, which can mislead farmers when satellite passes are delayed or weather stations are far away. We designed every telemetry card on AgroSync to explicitly communicate its data lineage and physical boundaries—clearly distinguishing modeled estimates from ground-station measurements, explaining that terrain slope is a screening proxy rather than an erosion probability, and transparently notifying users when surface soil moisture switches to a model fallback if NASA SMAP radiometer data is unavailable. Pairing this transparent scientific dashboard with a farmer Registration and Broadcast system further extends the reach of satellite data beyond individual dashboard users to entire farming communities.

Throughout development, our team prioritized four critical real-world factors: data resilience, spatial accuracy, rural connectivity, and agronomic safety. First, because satellite soil-moisture observations can experience spatial or temporal gaps, we engineered automatic model fallbacks so farmers always receive uninterrupted guidance. Second, recognizing that microclimates vary sharply across Ghana, we included explicit spatial disclaimers confirming that readings describe the farmer's selected point rather than the entire country. Third, we kept the codebase lean and static-friendly so pages load quickly on low-bandwidth mobile connections in rural areas. Finally, to ensure responsible decision-making, we designed AgroSync to complement—rather than replace—human expertise by prompting farmers to consult local MoFA extension officers before finalizing major crop-rotation changes.
